line: Hawaa counts the steps up a hill in sevens: 7, 14, 21.
Overnight, the temperature drops 4 degrees every hour, from 6 degrees, down past zero.
Here is how to do it.
Find the step: each number is 4 less than the one before. A sequence is a rule, used again and again. Find the rule first.
Keep taking 4 away, even below zero. From −2, count 4 more down the number line: −3, −4, −5, −6.
The missing number is −6. Check it: −6 is 4 less than −2.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A stadium says 352,741 people came this season. Someone asks: is that a lot of 5s?
There is one 5 in that number. But it is not worth five. It is worth fifty thousand.
Here is how to do it.
Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, hundred thousands. Always from the right. The right-hand end is where counting starts.

section: step 2 — 5 is in the ten thousands
line: The 5 is the fifth place along, which is ten thousands. Each step left multiplies by ten. That is the whole idea of place value.
So the 5 is worth 50,000. Same digit, different place, different worth. Move it and the number changes completely.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
An old clock in Freetown has Roman numerals instead of numbers.
Films show the year they were made in Roman numerals too: MMXXVI.
Here is how to do it.
X is 10 and L is 50. X before L means 50 take away 10. A smaller letter before a bigger one is taken away. That is the only trick.
I before V means 5 take away 1. IV, IX, XL, XC, CD and CM are the six take-away pairs.
Add the parts: 40 and 4 make 44. Read left to right in chunks, then add the chunks.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A school trip needs coaches. 187 children are going, and each coach holds 50.
Nobody says “about 187”. They say “about 200”. Rounding is saying a number the way people actually say it.
Here is how to do it.
To round to the nearest thousand, look at the digit one place to the right. That digit is the whole decision. Nothing to the right of it matters at all.
4 is less than 5, so the thousands stay as they are. It is nearer 3000 than 4000, and that is all rounding means: which is it closer to.
Everything after the thousands becomes zero. You are not deleting the digits, you are saying the number to the nearest thousand.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
It was 3 degrees at breakfast. By night it had dropped to 5 below zero.
How far did it fall? Not 2. It fell 3 to reach zero, then 5 more. Eight.
Here is how to do it.
From −5 up to 0 is five steps. Zero is the meeting point. Always go there first and the sign stops confusing you.
From 0 up to 3 is three more. The second half is ordinary counting. The minus sign was only ever in the first half.
Add the two halves: the gap is 8. Never subtract the two numbers. −5 and 3 are 8 apart, not 2.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: 24 tiles. Can you lay them in a perfect rectangle?

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6. Every rectangle you can make gives you two factors.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: Here is how to do it.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: Start at 1. Every number has 1 and itself. Working in pairs means you never miss one and never repeat one.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: Try 2, then 3, then 4. Each that works gives a pair. Stop when the pair crosses over. After 4×6 comes 6×4, which you already have.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: Eight factors. 5 is missing because 24 tiles will not make a rectangle five wide.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself. 1 is not prime: it has only one factor.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: Squared means times itself; cubed means three of it multiplied. 5² is not 10.

part: Multiples, factors, primes, squares and cubes
line: That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
In Labé it was −3 degrees before dawn. By noon it was 18 degrees.
A newspaper says 42,000 people came to the match. The real number was 41,768.
Here is how to do it.
Count up from −3 to zero: that is 3 degrees. Zero is a stepping stone. Getting there first makes the sum easy.
Then count on from zero to 18. Above zero it is ordinary counting.
Together the temperature rose 21 degrees. Rise is always counted going up, so the answer is positive.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Mariama has £4,600 saved and adds £2,700 more.
There is no need for columns. These numbers are friendly.
Here is how to do it.
3,999 is one less than 4,000. Numbers just below a round number are easier to round, then fix.
Add the round number. Adding thousands is quick in your head.
Take the 1 back off. You added one too many, so take it away again.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Two market stalls counted their takings: 2,456 and 1,837.
Too big to do in your head. Line them up so ones sit under ones.
Here is how to do it.
Start at the right. 13 is too big for one column. Only one digit fits in each column. The ten goes next door, where tens live.
Now the tens, and do not forget the one you carried. The carried digit is a real ten. Leaving it out loses ten from the answer.
Carry on left. The answer is 4,293. Check it roughly: 2500 and 1800 is about 4300. It is.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A shopkeeper adds up a bill: £3,189 + £2,906. Is £6,095 right?
A quick estimate catches big mistakes, and the inverse proves the answer.
Here is how to do it.
Round each number to the nearest hundred. Rounded numbers are easy to add in your head.
The answer should be about 6,100. 6,095 is close to 6,100, so it is sensible.
Check it exactly: take one number back off. Taking away undoes adding. If you get back where you started, the answer is right.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A stadium holds 48,500 people. 31,276 tickets are sold.
The question asks how many seats are left.
Here is how to do it.
Seats left means the total take away the seats sold. Look for the words that tell you which operation: left, more, fewer, altogether.
Use column subtraction. Line up the places and exchange where you need to.
Check by adding back. The inverse proves it.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Binta has 30 boxes of eggs. Seven eggs in every box.
She already knows 3 sevens are 21. Thirty boxes is ten times three boxes.
Here is how to do it.
Do the easy one first. Three sevens are 21. You are not learning a new fact. You are using one you have.
Thirty boxes is ten times as many as three boxes. Ten times bigger going in means ten times bigger coming out.
So 30 × 7 is 210. This is the most-asked thing in the whole test. It is worth doing until it is automatic.
Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left. The decimal point stays; the digits move.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A shop sells juice in crates of 6. There are 248 crates.
Break 248 into its columns and multiply each one, right to left.
Here is how to do it.
Ones first. 48 is four tens and eight. Same rule as adding: one digit per column, the rest moves left.
Tens next. Multiply, then add what you carried. Multiply first, add the carry after. Doing it the other way gives the wrong answer.
1,488 bottles. Roughly 250 × 6 = 1500, so 1,488 is believable.
For two digits, multiply by the 7, then by the 20, then add. The second row starts with a zero because it’s tens.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
852 sweets shared fairly between 4 children.
Work left to right this time — the opposite of adding. Share the biggest pieces first.
Here is how to do it.
Start at the left. 8 hundreds shared by 4 is 2 hundreds each. Division starts at the big end because that is how you actually share things out.
4 goes into 5 once, and 1 is left over. Carry it to the next digit. The leftover 1 is really 10, which is why it joins the next column.
The carried 1 makes 12. 12 ÷ 4 is 3. Each child gets 213. Check: 213 × 4 should give 852 back.
When it doesn’t divide exactly, what’s left is the remainder. The remainder is always smaller than what you divide by.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Tickets cost £4. You buy 3 and you already had £5.
5 + 3 × 4. Left to right gives 32. That is wrong — and it is wrong by a lot.
Here is how to do it.
Multiplication happens first, wherever it sits. × and ÷ bind more tightly than + and −. They grab their numbers first.
Then the addition. 17, not 32. Reading left to right is the single most expensive habit in arithmetic.
(5 + 3) × 4 = 32. Brackets say “do me first”. If you want the adding first, you have to say so with brackets.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
125 children are going on a trip to Kinkon. Each coach holds 40.
125 ÷ 40 doesn’t come out exactly. What do you do with the leftover?
Here is how to do it.
Three coaches hold 120 children, and 5 are left over. The remainder is real people, not a number to ignore.

section: step 2 — 5 children still need a seat
line: So you need another coach. When everyone must fit, round up.
4 coaches are needed. If the question were how many full coaches, the answer would be 3. Read what it asks.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Alfaa cuts a pizza into 8 slices and eats 4. Sara cuts hers into 2 and eats 1.
They ate the same amount: 4/8 and 1/2 are equivalent.
Here is how to do it.
Find the biggest number that goes into both: 6. Dividing top and bottom by the same number keeps the fraction the same size.
Divide the top and the bottom by 6. Do the same to both, always.
2/3 is the simplest form. Nothing else goes into 2 and 3, so it can’t be simplified further.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Two cups of juice: one is 3/4 full, the other is 5/8 full.
Which has more? The bottoms are different, so you can’t just look at the tops.
Here is how to do it.
Change 3/4 into eighths: multiply top and bottom by 2. Fractions are easy to compare when their bottoms match.
Now compare the tops: 6 is more than 5. Same-sized pieces, so more pieces means more juice.
So 3/4 is the greater fraction. A bigger bottom number means smaller pieces, not a bigger fraction.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A pizza cut into 8. You eat 3 slices, your brother eats 2.
3 slices and 2 slices is 5 slices. The slices did not change size.
Here is how to do it.
Add the top numbers. The top counts how many slices. That is the only thing changing.
The bottom says what size the slices are. It does not change. 8 + 8 = 16 would mean the slices got smaller, and nobody cut anything.
Five eighths of the pizza is gone. Adding bottoms is the commonest fraction mistake there is. Never do it.
Taking away works the same way: make the bottoms match first. Never take away the bottoms.
For mixed numbers, exchange a whole if the fraction is too small. One whole is 4/4, so 3 1/4 is 2 5/4.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
£60 in your pocket. You spend three quarters of it.
Split the 60 into 4 equal parts first. Then take three of them.
Here is how to do it.
Divide by the bottom number. That is one quarter. The bottom tells you how many pieces to cut the amount into.
Multiply by the top number. You want three of those quarters. Bottom first, then top. Doing it the other way round still works but the numbers get ugly.
Forty-five pounds spent. Three quarters should be most of it but not all. 45 out of 60 looks right.
For a shape, count the shaded parts over all the equal parts. Then simplify if you’re asked.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Half a chocolate bar. You give a third of that half away.
A third of a half is a sixth. “Of” means multiply, and the answer gets smaller.
Here is how to do it.
Multiply the top numbers together. No common bottom needed. This is the easiest of the four and it looks the hardest.
Multiply the bottom numbers together. The pieces get smaller, so the bottom number gets bigger. That is the sense of it.
One sixth of the bar. Multiplying two fractions always makes something smaller than both. That is your check.
Times by a whole number: multiply the top only. The bottom says the size of the pieces, which doesn’t change.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Three quarters of a pound is 75p, which is £0.75.
A fraction is a division waiting to happen.
Here is how to do it.
The fraction line means divide. Top divided by bottom always gives the decimal.
Use short division: 3.000 ÷ 8. Add zeros after the decimal point until it divides exactly.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Usumaani runs 100 metres in 14.36 seconds.
The results board shows times to one decimal place.
Here is how to do it.
One decimal place: draw a line after the tenths. Everything after the line will go.
Look at the next digit: 6. It is 5 or more. 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 stays.
Round the tenths up: 14.4 seconds. Never just cut the number off: 14.3 would be wrong.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
In the long jump, Hawaa jumps 3.6 metres and Ama jumps 3.58 metres.
3.58 has more digits. Does that mean it’s further?
Here is how to do it.
Give them the same number of decimal places. Adding a zero at the end doesn’t change a decimal.
Compare place by place: the ones match, then the tenths. The first place that differs decides it.
Hawaa jumped further. More digits doesn’t mean bigger.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Petrol is £1.40 a litre. You buy 6 litres.
Cover the point. Do 14 × 6. Then put the point back where it belongs.
Here is how to do it.
Pretend it is a whole number for a moment. Whole-number multiplication is something you can already do. Use it.

section: step 2 — one decimal place in, one out
line: 1.4 had one digit after the point, so the answer has one. Count the places you started with. That is exactly how many you end with.
£8.40 of petrol. Check roughly: 1.4 is nearly 1.5, and 1.5 × 6 = 9. Close enough to trust.
Short division with decimals: keep the decimal point in line. Dividing by 10 or 100 moves the digits to the right.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A drink at £1.45 and a sandwich at £2.30.
Line up the points, not the ends. That is the whole rule.
Here is how to do it.
Write them with the decimal points in a vertical line. The point is where the whole numbers stop. Line that up and every column is right.
If one has fewer digits, put zeros in the empty places. 3.5 is 3.50. The zero changes nothing except making the columns match.
Add as normal, and keep the point in line. The point in the answer sits directly under the others. Never move it.
To take away decimals, line up the points and fill gaps with zeros. 7.5 is the same as 7.50.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A shirt is half price. Another is 50% off. Another is 0.5 of the price.
All three shops are saying exactly the same thing in three different costumes.
Here is how to do it.
Divide the top by the bottom: 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. A fraction is a division waiting to happen. That is all the line means.
Multiply by 100. Per cent means out of a hundred. Decimal to percentage is always × 100. Two steps left, then a % sign.
1/4, 1/5, 3/4, 1/10 — know these without thinking. There are about eight worth memorising. They come up in every paper.
A percentage is a fraction out of 100. Simplify it. Divide top and bottom by 5.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A pair of trainers costs £60. The shop takes 15% off in the sale.
Per cent means “out of a hundred”. 15% means 15 for every 100.
Here is how to do it.
10% is one tenth. Divide by 10. 10% is the one you should never have to think about. Everything else is built from it.
5% is half of 10%. Half of 6 is 3. Halving is easier than dividing by 20, and it is the same thing.
15% is 10% and 5% together. £9 off. Any percentage can be built from 10%, 5% and 1%. You never need a formula.
For a sale price, find the percentage, then take it off. The amount taken off isn’t the answer.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Three bags of rice weigh 1.2 kg, 950 g and 1,150 g.
They use different units, so change them all to the same one first.
Here is how to do it.
Change kilograms to grams: × 1,000. 1 kg is 1,000 g.
Now they are all in grams. Same unit, so you can compare the numbers.
1,200 g is the largest. Always give the answer in the form the question used.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Mariama weighs flour on a kitchen scale. The pointer is between two numbers.
The trick is to work out what each little mark is worth.
Here is how to do it.
Between 0 and 100 there are 5 gaps, so each mark is 20. Count the gaps, not the marks.
The pointer is 3 marks along. Count from the last numbered mark.
So it reads 60 grams. Check it sits between the labelled numbers.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Alfaa buys a book for £3.45 and a pen for £1.80.
He pays with a £10 note. How much change?
Here is how to do it.
Add the prices, lining up the decimal points. Pounds under pounds, pence under pence.
Write £10 as £10.00, then take away. The zeros hold the pence places.
His change is £4.75. Check: £5.25 + £4.75 = £10.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
The bus leaves Dugun at 08:50 and reaches the market at 09:35.
How long is the journey? Time doesn’t work in hundreds.
Here is how to do it.
Count on to the next hour first. An hour has 60 minutes, so jump to the hour.
Then count on to the time. From an o’clock it’s easy to read.
The journey takes 45 minutes. Subtracting 850 from 935 gives 85, which is wrong: time isn’t base 10.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A bottle says 1.5 litres. The recipe asks for millilitres.
Milli means a thousandth. So one litre is a thousand of them.
Here is how to do it.
Know the four that matter: km–m, m–cm, kg–g, l–ml. Three of those four are × 1000. Only m to cm is × 100.
Going to a smaller unit means more of them, so multiply. Ask yourself: is the answer going to be bigger or smaller? Then you cannot pick the wrong way.
Fifteen hundred millilitres. 1.5 litres could never be 0.0015 of anything. The size check catches the slip.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A road sign in England says Oxford 20 miles.
In Guinea, distances are in kilometres. How far is that?
Here is how to do it.
Remember: 5 miles is about 8 kilometres. The SATs give this fact or expect you to know it.
20 miles is 4 lots of 5 miles. Find how many groups of 5.
So it is about 32 kilometres. A kilometre is shorter than a mile, so there are more of them.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A garden 8 metres long and 5 metres wide. How much turf?
Picture it as rows of one-metre squares: 5 rows of 8.
Here is how to do it.
Area is just counting squares, arranged in rows. That is why it is length times width — it is a multiplication table drawn out.
Forty squares. Do not add. 8 + 5 = 13 is the perimeter's half, not the area.
Square metres, because you counted squares. The little 2 is not decoration. An answer in m instead of m² loses the mark.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round: add every side. Area is the space inside. Don’t mix them up.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A box 4 cm by 3 cm by 5 cm. How many centimetre cubes fit?
Fill the bottom layer first, then count how many layers.
Here is how to do it.
Twelve cubes cover the base. The base is just an area. You already know how to do that bit.
The box is 5 cubes tall. Volume is area with a third dimension stacked on top of it.
Sixty cubic centimetres. Little 3 this time, because you counted cubes rather than squares.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A jug holds 2 litres of juice. Hawaa pours 6 glasses of 250 ml.
How much is left in the jug?
Here is how to do it.
Put everything in the same unit: millilitres. You can’t take millilitres from litres directly.
Work out how much was poured. One step at a time.
500 ml is left. Check the answer is less than the jug held.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A dice is a cube. A tent can be a triangular prism.
Shapes have faces, edges and vertices you can count.
Here is how to do it.
Two triangle ends and three rectangle sides. Faces are the flat surfaces.
Three round each triangle, and three joining them. Edges are where two faces meet.
Three corners on each triangle. Vertices are the corners.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A kite, a rhombus and a trapezium are all quadrilaterals: four sides.
What makes them different is their sides and angles.
Here is how to do it.
It is a quadrilateral. Count the sides first.
Only one pair of sides are parallel. Parallel lines never meet, like railway lines.
One pair of parallel sides makes a trapezium. Two pairs would make a parallelogram.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Flatten a cereal box and you get its net: the shape that folds up into the box.
Every face of the box is one piece of the net.
Here is how to do it.
Two triangles make the two ends. Matching end faces mean a prism.
Three rectangles join the ends. A triangle has three sides, so three rectangles.
It folds into a triangular prism. Count the faces and name the end shape.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A door swings open. How far did it turn?
Three facts cover almost every angle question: a line is 180°, a point is 360°, a triangle is 180°.
Here is how to do it.
Angles sitting on a straight line always add to 180. Half a full turn. If you can picture the turn, you never have to remember the number.
Subtract what you have from what it should be. Every missing-angle question is a subtraction once you know which total to use.
And it should look like an acute angle. Check the picture agrees. If your answer is 150° but the angle looks tiny, you have used the wrong total.
Angles around a point add up to 360°. A full turn is 360°.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Draw a circle with a compass. The point is the centre.
The radius goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across.
Here is how to do it.
The diameter is two radiuses end to end. It passes through the centre.
Double the radius. Halve the diameter to get the radius.
The diameter is 14 cm. The diameter is always the longer one.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Fold a picture of a butterfly down the middle. The halves match.
The fold is a line of symmetry.
Here is how to do it.
Fold from each corner to the opposite corner. Each fold that matches is a line of symmetry.
Fold from the middle of each side to the opposite side. Check every way, not just one.
A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry. A regular shape has as many lines as it has sides.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A counter on a grid slides 3 squares right and 2 squares down.
That is a translation: the shape moves but doesn’t turn.
Here is how to do it.
Right adds to the x-coordinate. x is across, the first number.
Down takes away from the y-coordinate. y is up, the second number. It can go below zero.
The new point is (5, −1). Reflection is different: in the x-axis, y changes sign; in the y-axis, x does.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A map of Conakry has a grid. A point is found by going across, then up.
Some points are left of zero or below it.
Here is how to do it.
Go across first: 3 to the left of zero, so −3. Along the corridor, then up the stairs.
Then up: 2. Below the x-axis would be negative.
Write x first, then y, in brackets. (2, −3) would be a different point.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Cerno’s recipe for rice for 4 people uses 300 g of rice.
He’s cooking for 12. How much rice?
Here is how to do it.
12 people is 3 times as many as 4. Find how many times bigger.
So use 3 times as much rice. Everything in the recipe scales by the same amount.
He needs 900 g of rice. Adding 8 to the grams would be wrong: ratios multiply.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Ama got 18 out of 25 on one test and 34 out of 50 on another.
Which test did she do better on? The totals are different.
Here is how to do it.
Make the bottom 100: 25 × 4 = 100. Percent means out of 100.
Do the same to the top. Same fraction, new form.
18 out of 25 is 72%. 34 out of 50 is 68%, so the first was better. Percentages put scores on the same scale.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A photo is 4 cm by 6 cm. It is enlarged by a scale factor of 3.
Every side gets three times longer.
Here is how to do it.
Multiply the short side by 3. A scale factor multiplies every length.
Multiply the long side by 3. The same factor, every side.
The new photo is 12 cm by 18 cm. To find a scale factor, divide a new side by its old side.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
30 sweets shared between two brothers, 3 for one and 2 for the other each time.
Count the shares first. 3 and 2 makes 5 shares, not 2.
Here is how to do it.
Add the numbers in the ratio to find how many shares there are. This step is the one everybody skips, and skipping it makes every answer wrong.
Divide the total by the number of shares. One share is 6. Now you know what a single share is worth, and the rest is multiplying.
18 and 12. They add back to 30. Always add your two answers back. If they do not make the total, something is wrong.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A crate holds 3 equal sacks of rice. With the 4 kg crate, it all weighs 19 kg.
Use a letter for what you don’t know. Each sack is n kg, so 3n + 4 = 19.
Here is how to do it.
Take away the 4 from both sides. Undo the last thing done to n first.
Then divide by 3. 3n means 3 × n, so divide to undo it.
n is 5. Check: 3 × 5 + 4 = 19.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A recipe: cook a chicken for 40 minutes per kilogram, plus 20 minutes.
In maths that is written t = 40w + 20. The letter is just a box waiting for a number.
Here is how to do it.
Swap the letter for the number you were given. 3x means 3 times x. The multiplication sign is hidden, not missing.
Multiply first, because × comes before +. The order of operations still applies. It always applies.
So y is 17. Algebra is arithmetic with a gap in it. Fill the gap and it is ordinary sums.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Tables in a hall: 1 table seats 6, 2 tables seat 10, 3 tables seat 14.
How many seats for 20 tables? Find the rule.
Here is how to do it.
The sequence goes up by 4. The step tells you the multiplier.
4 × 1 = 4, and the first term is 6, so add 2. Test the rule on the first term.
The 20th term is 82. Check with the second term: 4 × 2 + 2 = 10.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Two numbers. They add to 7. They multiply to 12.
Do not guess wildly. List the pairs that multiply to 12 and check which adds to 7.
Here is how to do it.
Start with the multiplying, because there are fewer options. Multiplication narrows things down fast. Addition has far too many pairs.
Check each pair against the second fact. Two facts about two numbers is always enough. You just have to use both.
The numbers are 3 and 4. Test them both ways before you write anything down.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A café has 3 sandwiches and 4 drinks.
How many different meals of one sandwich and one drink?
Here is how to do it.
Each sandwich can go with any of the 4 drinks. List one row to see the pattern.
There are 3 sandwiches, so 3 rows. A table of rows and columns shows every pair.
12 different meals. Adding 3 + 4 would miss most of them.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A bar chart shows how many children in a class chose each fruit.
The scale goes up in 2s, so not every value has a line.
Here is how to do it.
Read the scale: each line is 2. Always check the scale first.
The bar stops halfway between 6 and 8. Halfway between two lines is one more than the lower.
So 7 children chose it. For a pie chart, use fractions of the circle instead.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
A table shows the boys and girls at three schools.
The question asks how many children at Labé school altogether.
Here is how to do it.
Find Labé in the table. Read across the row, not down the column.
Altogether means add the boys and girls. Look for the word that tells you the operation.
42 children altogether. Check you used the right row and the right numbers.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
Three fish weighed 5 kg, 3 kg and 10 kg.
The mean is what each would weigh if you shared the weight out evenly.
Here is how to do it.
Add them all together. You are pooling everything before sharing it back out.
Divide by how many there were. Count how many, not how big. Three fish means divide by three.
Six kilograms each, if they were all the same. The mean sits between the smallest and the biggest. If yours does not, check again.
That is the whole method. Try one yourself.
